title: async/await without blocking
summary: Model I/O as asynchronous work, keep the UI responsive, and avoid the classic deadlocks.

workedExample.title: Sequential vs concurrent awaits
steps: In version A, the first await suspends until `a` completes. Only then does the method start fetching `b`. Total time is roughly the sum of both calls.
In version B, `FetchAsync("a")` begins and returns a `Task<string>` immediately; the method does not await yet. The same happens for `b`.
`Task.WhenAll` waits for both tasks and returns their results in input order. The two I/O operations overlap, so total time is roughly the slower of the two.
If either task throws, the awaited `WhenAll` throws, exposing one of the exceptions. Use `await Task.WhenAll` and handle failures deliberately.
Concurrency is appropriate only when the operations are independent and the downstream system can handle the load. Do not fire unbounded parallelism.

bugFix.title: The blocking call inside async
bugFix.explanation: `.Result` blocks the current thread while the I/O is in flight. In a synchronization-context environment, the continuation may need that same thread, producing a deadlock; even without a deadlock, a thread is wasted. Make the method `async Task<string>` and `await` the call: `public async Task<string> LoadProfileAsync(int userId, CancellationToken ct = default) => await _http.GetStringAsync($"/users/{userId}", ct);`. Async should flow through the call chain.

explainPrompt: Explain what `await` does to the current thread, and why `.Result` on an async task is dangerous. When would you use `Task.WhenAll`?

checkQuestions.prompt: What happens when an async method awaits an incomplete I/O task?
options: The thread blocks until the task finishes
The method returns a Task to its caller and resumes later
The runtime creates a new OS thread for every await
The task runs synchronously on the same thread
checkQuestions.explanation: `await` suspends the method and returns control to the caller; a continuation resumes the method when the operation completes.
optionExplanations: Awaiting is non-blocking for the calling thread.
A new thread is not created per await; continuations are scheduled when needed.
I/O completion does not require the same thread to sit and wait.

checkQuestions.prompt: Why is `.Result` dangerous in async code?
options: It blocks a thread and can deadlock with a synchronization context
It only works for value types
checkQuestions.explanation: Blocking on an async operation can deadlock and causes thread-pool starvation under load.
optionExplanations: The type is usually correct; the waiting behavior is the problem.

options: When operations are independent and can safely run concurrently
When each operation depends on the previous result
When you want to ignore exceptions
When you need a synchronous return value
checkQuestions.explanation: `WhenAll` overlaps independent asynchronous operations and waits for all of them.
optionExplanations: Dependent operations must be awaited in sequence.
`WhenAll` surfaces failures; it does not hide exceptions.
It returns an awaitable, not a synchronous value.
